questions.stem: A co-operative is a business that is:
options: owned by shareholders, with votes based on the shares each holds
owned by one person, who has unlimited liability for its debts
owned by the government to provide services to the public
owned and controlled by its members, with one vote per member
questions.explanation: In a co-operative, voting rights attach to membership rather than shareholding, so each member generally has one vote whatever their investment. Votes in proportion to shares describe a company.

questions.stem: Which group would be best suited to forming a co-operative?
options: dairy farmers who want to jointly own a plant to process their milk
a graphic designer who works alone from a studio at her home
a large mining company raising funds from thousands of new investors
a franchisee running a single outlet of a fast-food chain
questions.explanation: Co-operatives suit groups with a shared need who want to own and control a business together and share its benefits, such as farmers pooling their produce. A sole operator or a large investor-owned firm suits other structures.

questions.stem: Two partners in Bathurst are considering incorporating their business as a company. Which is a cost of incorporation they should weigh up?
options: personal liability of the owners for all of the company's debts
having to charge customers GST at a higher rate than before
losing the right to trade under a registered business name
more set-up costs and ongoing reporting obligations with ASIC
questions.explanation: A company is a separate legal entity with limited liability, but it costs more to set up and run, with ASIC registration, annual review fees and its own tax return. Incorporation reduces, not increases, owners' personal liability.

questions.stem: An Australian Business Number (ABN) is:
options: a number given only to the companies listed on the ASX
a unique 11-digit number that identifies a business
a licence that allows a business to sell alcohol
a registration that stops rivals copying a name
questions.explanation: An ABN is an 11-digit identifier issued free by the Australian Business Register to those carrying on an enterprise. Protecting a name from copying requires a registered trade mark.

questions.stem: Which sole trader must register a business name with ASIC?
options: Ana Lopez, trading as 'Harbour City Tiling'
Ana Lopez, trading under the name 'Ana Lopez'
Sam Ng, trading under the name 'Sam Ng'
Lee Park, trading under the name 'Lee Park'
questions.explanation: A business name must be registered unless an individual trades under their own first name and surname and nothing else. 'Harbour City Tiling' is a different trading name, so it must be registered.

questions.stem: Jack Brown, a sole trader, trades as 'Jack Brown & Co'. Must he register a business name?
options: yes, because he has added words to his own name
no, because the name includes his first and last name
no, because only companies register business names
yes, but only once he employs more than 15 staff
questions.explanation: The exemption applies only when an individual uses their first name and surname and nothing else, so adding '& Co' means the name must be registered with ASIC. Sole traders, partnerships and companies may all need to register names.

questions.stem: Why does a new business apply for an ABN?
options: so its owners gain limited liability for all of the business's debts
so its brand is legally protected from use by its competitors
so it no longer has to pay any income tax on its business profits
so it can register for GST and a business name, and quote it on invoices
questions.explanation: An ABN identifies the business to government and others: it is needed to register a business name and for GST, and it appears on invoices. It does not change liability, protect a brand or remove tax.

questions.stem: A Tamworth business with an active ABN, registered as 'Tamworth Crust Bakery', wants the domain tamworthcrust.com.au. Why is it allowed to hold this domain?
options: a .com.au domain can be held by any person anywhere in the world
every domain must include 'Pty Ltd' to be accepted for registration
the local council has approved the domain as part of its permit
it is an Australian business and the domain matches words in its name
questions.explanation: A .com.au domain requires an Australian commercial presence, such as an active ABN, and a connection between the domain and the registrant, such as matching words from its name in the same order. Councils play no part in domain names.

questions.stem: Start-up costs are best described as:
options: regular costs paid once the business is trading, such as weekly wages
the profit the owner expects to earn in the first year of trading
the tax the business must pay at the end of its first financial year
costs of getting the business ready to open, such as fit-out and first stock
questions.explanation: Start-up costs are incurred before or at opening: premises fit-out, equipment, initial inventory, bonds and registrations. Wages and bills paid once trading are operating costs.

questions.stem: Which is a start-up cost for a new cafe in Orange?
options: the monthly electricity bills once the cafe is operating
the interest paid on its bank loan in the third year
the espresso machine and the first stock of coffee beans
the weekly wages paid to staff after six months of trading
questions.explanation: Equipment and initial inventory are needed before the cafe can open, so they are start-up costs. The other items are ongoing operating costs.

questions.stem: A planned Lismore bike shop budgets for a fit-out of $45,000, equipment of $28,000, initial inventory of $12,000, a lease bond of $8,000 and monthly rent of $4,000 once trading. What are its total start-up costs?
questions.explanation: $45,000 + $28,000 + $12,000 + $8,000 = $93,000. Monthly rent paid once trading is an operating cost, so adding it gives the wrong total of $97,000.

questions.stem: Why should a new business's start-up funding include a cash buffer for its first few months of operating costs?
options: a cash buffer removes the need for any cash flow forecast
sales are often low at first while rent and wages must still be paid
operating costs are only paid after the first year of trading ends
lenders will not lend money to any business that holds spare cash
questions.explanation: It takes time to build a customer base, but costs such as rent, wages and supplier bills start at once, so many new businesses fail from running out of cash. A buffer gives time to grow, alongside a cash flow forecast.

questions.stem: Under the superannuation guarantee, from 1 July 2025 an employer must contribute:
options: 9.5% of wages, and only for workers who are full-time
12% of each eligible worker's ordinary time earnings
10% of each eligible worker's ordinary time earnings
12% of the business's net profit at the end of the year
questions.explanation: The super guarantee rate rose to 12% of ordinary time earnings from 1 July 2025, its final scheduled increase. It is based on employees' earnings, not the business's profit, and applies to casual and part-time employees too.

questions.stem: A new business hires an employee on a base salary of $65,000 a year. Counting only salary and the 12% superannuation guarantee, what is the annual cost of this employee?
questions.explanation: Super = 12% x $65,000 = $7,800, so the cost is $65,000 + $7,800 = $72,800. Super is paid by the employer on top of the salary, not deducted from it, which is the slip that gives $57,200.

questions.stem: Under the National Employment Standards, a full-time employee is entitled each year to:
options: 4 weeks of unpaid annual leave and 10 days of unpaid sick leave
4 weeks of paid annual leave and 10 days of paid personal/carer's leave
2 weeks of paid annual leave and 5 days of paid personal/carer's leave
6 weeks of paid annual leave and 15 days of paid personal/carer's leave
questions.explanation: The NES give full-time employees 4 weeks of paid annual leave (pro rata for part-time) and 10 days of paid personal/carer's leave. Employers must plan for this paid time off and for covering staff on leave.

questions.stem: Under the National Employment Standards, casual employees:
options: do not receive paid annual leave or paid personal/carer's leave
receive 4 weeks of paid annual leave like full-time employees
receive 10 days of paid sick leave after one month of work
are not covered by any of the minimum employment entitlements at all
questions.explanation: Casuals are not entitled to paid annual or personal/carer's leave and usually receive a higher hourly rate instead. They still have some NES entitlements, such as unpaid carer's leave.

questions.stem: A Newcastle cafe owner is choosing between a full-time barista and several casual baristas. Which statement is correct?
options: casuals cost less because employers pay no super for casual staff
full-time staff are cheaper because their annual leave is unpaid
casuals must be given 4 weeks of paid annual leave each year
casuals usually cost more per hour but let staffing match demand
questions.explanation: Casuals usually receive a higher hourly rate instead of paid leave, but rosters can be matched to busy and quiet times. Employers must pay the super guarantee for casual employees as well.

questions.stem: Which is part of the full cost of employing a worker, on top of wages?
options: superannuation, paid leave and workers compensation insurance
the owner's own personal income tax bill for the whole financial year
the GST the business collects from its customers on sales
the council rates charged on the owner's private home
questions.explanation: Labour costs include wages plus super, paid leave and workers compensation insurance premiums. GST collected belongs to the ATO and is not a labour cost.

questions.stem: A new Wollongong bakery needs bakers from 3 am every day and extra sales staff on busy weekend mornings. Which labour plan best suits these needs?
options: no employees, with the owner working every shift alone
permanent bakers, plus casual sales staff for the weekend peaks
casual bakers who are called in only when the shop is already busy
full-time sales staff rostered on every day of the week
questions.explanation: Baking is needed every day, so permanent staff give reliability and skill, while casuals cover predictable peaks without paying for idle time. Calling bakers in only when busy would leave no bread to sell.

questions.stem: Crowdfunding involves:
options: raising small amounts from many people, usually online
borrowing a large sum from one bank over many years
selling some of the business's equipment to raise extra cash
using profits kept in the business from earlier years
questions.explanation: Crowdfunding platforms let a business raise money from many supporters, who may receive rewards, early products or shares. A large bank loan is traditional debt finance.

questions.stem: Peer-to-peer lending is a fintech source of finance in which a business:
options: uses the owner's personal savings to buy its equipment
borrows from individual investors through an online platform
sells shares to the public through the stock exchange
receives money from the government that is never repaid
questions.explanation: Peer-to-peer platforms match borrowers directly with people who lend money, often with quicker approval than a bank. It is still debt, so it must be repaid with interest.

questions.stem: How does a government grant differ from a bank loan for a new business?
options: a grant is available to every new business that applies for one
a grant generally need not be repaid but has eligibility conditions
a grant must be repaid with a higher rate of interest than a loan
a grant gives the government part ownership of the business
questions.explanation: Grants are usually non-repayable funds for specific purposes, such as innovation or exporting, but they are competitive and come with conditions. Loans must be repaid with interest.

questions.stem: A start-up raises $300,000 from 600 investors in exchange for shares, using an ASIC-licensed crowd-sourced funding platform. Compared with a bank loan, the main disadvantage is that:
options: the business must offer its premises as security for the funds
the funds can be spent only on inventory for the first year
the founders give up part of their ownership and future profits
the money must be repaid with interest in monthly instalments
questions.explanation: Equity crowd-sourced funding sells shares, so the founders share ownership and future profits with investors. There are no loan repayments, which is the advantage over debt.

questions.stem: What is the main advantage for an owner of using personal savings to start a business?
options: the owner's risk of loss is shared with the bank
the amount available is unlimited for any owner
the savings are repaid by the government if lost
no interest is paid and no ownership is given up
questions.explanation: Savings avoid interest and keep full control with the owner, but the owner bears the whole risk and the amount is limited to what has been saved.

questions.stem: An invoice states payment terms of 'net 30 days'. This means the customer:
options: must pay 30 days before goods are sent
must pay the full amount within 30 days
must pay a 30% deposit before delivery
receives a 30% discount for paying cash
questions.explanation: Payment terms set when an invoice must be paid; 'net 30' means the full amount is due within 30 days of the invoice date. Discounts for early payment are a separate term.

questions.stem: A new wholesaler gives customers 60 days to pay, but its own suppliers require payment within 14 days. What is the main risk?
options: lost profit, because credit sales do not count as revenue
cash shortages, because cash goes out well before it comes in
lower sales, because customers dislike long payment terms
higher GST, because longer payment terms increase the tax rate
questions.explanation: Paying suppliers sooner than customers pay creates a cash gap that must be funded, even if sales are profitable. Credit sales still count as revenue; the issue is timing of cash.

questions.stem: A business offers customers a 2% discount if they pay an invoice within 7 days. The main aim is to:
options: encourage faster payment and improve cash flow
increase the GST collected on each of its sales
avoid having to issue a tax invoice to customers
lengthen the time customers take to pay invoices
questions.explanation: An early payment discount gives up a little revenue to receive cash sooner, reducing the risk of late payment and bad debts. It has no effect on GST obligations or invoicing rules.

questions.stem: A GST-registered business makes a sale of $500 including GST. Which details must its tax invoice include?
options: the buyer's home address and date of birth for checking
only the total price, with no other details required
its identity and ABN, the date, a description and the GST
the buyer's tax file number and the buyer's own bank details
questions.explanation: For sales under $1,000, a tax invoice must show that it is a tax invoice, the seller's identity and ABN, the date, what was sold with quantity and price, and the GST (or that the price includes GST). Tax file numbers never appear on invoices.

questions.stem: A GST-registered business invoices another business $2,200 including GST. Compared with a $500 sale, what extra must its tax invoice show?
options: the buyer's identity or ABN
the buyer's tax file number
a 10% discount on the price
nothing, as GST is not charged
questions.explanation: For sales of $1,000 or more, a tax invoice must also show the buyer's identity or ABN. The GST in this price is $2,200 / 11 = $200; sales to businesses are still taxable.

questions.stem: The role of insurance in managing financial risk is to:
options: provide a loan that is repaid only if the business succeeds
transfer the cost of specified losses to an insurer for a premium
guarantee that the business will make a profit every year
remove the need for any safety procedures in the workplace
questions.explanation: In return for regular premiums, an insurer pays for losses covered by the policy, so one event such as a fire or lawsuit does not ruin the business. Insurance does not replace good risk management.

questions.stem: A customer slips on a wet floor in a Manly gift shop and sues the business for her injuries. Which insurance covers this claim?
options: workers compensation insurance
income protection insurance
stock and contents insurance
public liability insurance
questions.explanation: Public liability insurance covers claims by members of the public injured, or whose property is damaged, because of the business. Workers compensation covers employees injured at work.

questions.stem: Most NSW businesses that employ staff must hold workers compensation insurance. This insurance:
options: covers stock that is stolen from the business
covers the owner's income if the business fails
covers injured workers' wages and medical costs
covers customers who are injured on the premises
questions.explanation: Workers compensation pays injured employees' lost wages and medical and rehabilitation costs, and is compulsory for most NSW employers. Customer injuries fall under public liability insurance.

questions.stem: To save a $1,200 annual premium, the owner of a new Albury hardware store decides not to insure its $150,000 of stock. Which evaluation is most valid?
options: the saving is worthwhile because stock losses are always tax deductible
the decision is sound because insurance covers only employee injuries
the risk is nil because hardware stock cannot be damaged or stolen
a fire or theft could cost far more than the premium and close the store
questions.explanation: Insurance trades a small certain cost for protection against a large uncertain loss; losing $150,000 of stock could end a new business. Tax deductions recover only part of a loss.

questions.stem: Goods and services tax (GST) in Australia is:
options: a 12% tax on the wages paid to employees
a 10% tax on most goods and services sold
a 30% tax on the profits of all companies
a tax paid by local councils on their land
questions.explanation: GST is a 10% tax on most goods, services and other items sold or consumed in Australia, collected by registered businesses and paid to the ATO. Company tax is levied on profits.

questions.stem: A business must register for GST when:
options: its net profit reaches $75,000 or more
its GST turnover reaches $150,000 or more
it employs its first full-time worker
its GST turnover reaches $75,000 or more
questions.explanation: The registration threshold is based on turnover (gross business income, excluding GST) of $75,000 or more, not profit. The $150,000 threshold applies to non-profit organisations.

questions.stem: How is the profit of a sole trader's business taxed?
options: the business pays company tax on all of it at a flat rate of 25%
the business pays GST on its profit instead of income tax
the profit is not taxed until the business is sold
the owner pays individual income tax on it at personal rates
questions.explanation: A sole trader is not a separate legal entity, so business profit is included in the owner's personal income tax return. Company tax applies only to companies.

questions.stem: How is the profit of a partnership taxed?
options: the partnership itself pays company tax on all of the profit
only the partner with the largest share pays any tax
the profit is taxed only when it is kept in the business
each partner pays income tax on their share of the profit
questions.explanation: A partnership lodges its own tax return to report its income but does not pay income tax itself; each partner pays tax on their share at personal rates.

questions.stem: A private company with an aggregated turnover of $3 million, earned almost entirely from trading, qualifies as a base rate entity. Its company tax rate is:
questions.explanation: Companies with aggregated turnover under $50 million and no more than 80% passive income are base rate entities taxed at 25%. Other companies pay the full rate of 30%.

questions.stem: A company that is a base rate entity has a taxable income of $240,000. How much company tax does it pay?
questions.explanation: 25% x $240,000 = $60,000. The full rate of 30% would give $72,000, and $180,000 is the profit left after tax.

questions.stem: Council rates are:
options: a fee paid to ASIC each year to keep a business name registered
a charge paid to the ATO on each employee's wages
a local council charge on owners of property in its area
a federal tax charged on every business's total sales
questions.explanation: Councils levy rates on landowners to fund local services such as roads and waste collection. A business that owns its premises pays them, and a tenant may contribute through its lease.
